p.x:
Last week, I bought some new headphones online. When the parcel arrived, I was very happy. But when I opened it, one side of the headphones didn't work!
I called the shop. "I'm sorry to complain," I said, "but my headphones are broken." The woman on the phone was very kind. "We're sorry," she said. "Can you send them back, please? We will fix them or send you new ones."
I sent them back the next day. The shop was very quick. Three days later, I received a new pair. I wrote an email to say, "Thanks for your help!" Now I always buy from that shop.

Everyone sometimes buys something faulty or receives poor service. Here's how to complain and get results.
Stay calm. When a product arrives damaged or a courier loses your parcel, it's natural to feel frustrated or even furious. But shouting rarely helps. Be polite but firm.
Contact customer service quickly. Many companies have a hotline, though you may be on hold for a long time. Email or online chat is often faster. Keep your message brief: explain what happened, when, and what you want.
Have the right information. Keep your proof of purchase, such as a receipt or order confirmation, and your tracking number if the problem is a delivery. When you contact the company, they'll give you a reference number. Write it down!
Know what you want. Do you want a refund, a replacement or a repair? If the product is defective and your warranty is still valid, the company should fix or replace it. If you're dissatisfied with the answer, say clearly that the situation is unacceptable and ask to speak to a manager.
Follow up. If nobody replies within a week, follow up with another email. If the company resolves the problem well, you might even get an apology and a voucher. Finally, leave an honest rating online to help other customers.

Complaining is often seen as negative, yet businesses increasingly regard complaints as valuable information. A customer who takes the time to explain a grievance is giving the company an opportunity to improve, and research suggests that customers whose problems are resolved swiftly often become more loyal than those who never had a problem at all.
The way a complaint is made, however, has a significant impact on the result. Experts recommend a concise, factual message with a calm tone. Emotional or aggressive language may make staff defensive, while a clear account of what went wrong, what evidence exists and what outcome is expected allows them to act. It also helps to acknowledge any steps the company has already taken before explaining why they are not enough.
If the first response is unsatisfactory, customers can escalate the complaint to a senior manager or a specialist department. In many countries, independent bodies such as an ombudsman can investigate complaints that companies fail to address, and consumer rights laws guarantee some form of redress, such as a repair, replacement or refund, when goods are faulty.
Companies, for their part, may offer a goodwill gesture, such as a discount or store credit, even when they are not legally required to. Such gestures can turn an unhappy customer into a loyal one. In an age when a single negative review can be seen by thousands, handling complaints well is not just good manners; it is good business.
